note: Hand-maintained. Generated by nobody, on purpose: a row here is an act of judgement, and a generator that could emit one could invent an owner. Checked by forensics/tools/prerequisite_gate.py, which requires `covers` to equal exactly the set of names it observed and refuses a row that keeps covering a name the crate has since built.

rule: deferrals: a name the crate references, or an authority unit calls, that no stratum has built yet. A row needs the stratum that will build it, a reason, and an evidence citation that can be read. A deferral is discharged by building the name, at which point the gate reports it as stale until the row is removed.
divergences: a name an authority unit calls that the crate deliberately does not, with the class of the difference and the reason. `covers` is exact in both directions.

units: an authority translation unit a subphase plan names, which no transcription edge, no built internal function, no referenced identifier and no symbol record reaches. Each row carries a class from a fixed set, and the class names the fields the row must prove, so the row can be falsified rather than believed. Forensics tools plan_reconciliation.py is the reader, and it also reports a row that covers a unit no plan row names.

divergences.note: The crate names this threads_common::clean_local. It was defined there and called from nowhere until the prerequisite gate's first run reported it: crypto/initthread.c's OPENSSL_thread_stop ends with CRYPTO_THREAD_clean_local(), the crate's version did not, and no scan of the crate alone could have seen it, because the crate's identifier and the authority's name are different and the call was simply absent. The call is now in OPENSSL_thread_stop, and the unit test a_thread_stop_drops_the_per_context_thread_locals pins the consequence rather than the call. Recorded as a divergence because the crate does build the function, so a deferral would have been stale the moment it was written; the row is what keeps this call from being deleted again without someone reading why it is there.

The crate drops the ossl_ prefix from this stratum's internal accessors: lib_ctx_default_deinit, lib_ctx_get_concrete, lib_ctx_get_data, lib_ctx_is_default_symbol, lib_ctx_is_global_default, lib_ctx_read_lock, lib_ctx_write_lock, lib_ctx_unlock and release_default_drbg_ctx are the same functions under those names. The prefix is dropped because these are pub(crate) Rust functions with no symbol, so the authority's name would only be a spelling with no ABI consequence; every authority *export* keeps its name verbatim, which is what ABI-PROTOTYPE resolves against. Each function's doc comment names the authority function it transcribes.
divergences.evidence: src/context/mod.rs, the doc comment above each of those definitions

divergences.note: Three one-line authority accessors with no single Rust counterpart. ossl_lib_ctx_get_ex_data_global is `ossl_lib_ctx_get_data(ctx, OSSL_LIB_CTX_EX_DATA_GLOBAL_INDEX)` in the authority, and the crate reaches that slot through lib_ctx_get_data; ossl_lib_ctx_is_child reads the ischild field, which the crate declares and reads in the same two places OSSL_LIB_CTX_free does; ossl_lib_ctx_get_descriptor answers a diagnostic string the crate does not have a caller for, and not inventing one is the reason it is recorded here rather than written.

Neither needs a function in the crate. On this profile openssl_init_fork_handlers() is `return 1` -- a no-op, which src/runtime/init.rs already records for OPENSSL_INIT_ATFORK -- and openssl_get_fork_id() is `return getpid()`, so a caller that needs a fork id asks the C library for one.

Each of these is a name the authority's *non-installed* headers introduce -- `#define F(x)` in crypto/md4/md4_local.h and crypto/sha/sha_local.h, `u8`/`u16`/`u32`/`u64` in crypto/aes/aes_local.h, macro-body and parameter names in include/internal/list.h, quic_*.h and sha3.h, and `sleep` in include/internal/e_os.h, which is EINTR-retry shim over the C library's -- and each also appears in this crate as an ordinary Rust identifier: a generic parameter, a local binding, a width alias, or a word inside a doc comment. A lexical scan of either side cannot separate those two facts, which is why this is a recorded class rather than a narrower matcher: a matcher tuned to drop `u8` would also drop a real collision. The gate holds the list exact, so a new member has to be looked at.
divergences.evidence: forensics/atlas/macro-owners.json (defined_in for each name); the gate's first-run report, recorded in docs/DECISIONS.md D123

units.reason: `crypto/provider.c` is the twenty-two `OSSL_PROVIDER_*` exports and nothing else -- it has no authority-internal function of its own -- so internal-symbols.json records zero names for it and transcription-edges.json attributes the module that defines them to `crypto/provider_core.c`, which dominates it. The unit is therefore reached and cannot be seen to be reached by any of the three mechanical signals, so the whole export list is named here and the claim is checkable: plan_reconciliation.py fails this row if any of the twenty-two is not in the implemented surface.

The file's content is `ossl_predefined_providers` -- a variable and not a function -- so internal-symbols.json has the name but the crate spells it `PREDEFINED_PROVIDERS` and no lexical signal pairs them. Named here so the claim is explicit rather than resting on a reader's memory.

The file is a single configuration-module list -- `ossl_config_modules[]`, a variable -- and the function that walks it, `OPENSSL_load_builtin_modules`. internal-symbols.json records neither, because the first is a variable and the second is an export. The exported half is named here, and it is what RT-CONF-MOD observes.

The file's only function is `ossl_err_load_DSO_strings`, which is not an export: the public `ERR_load_DSO_strings` is `crypto/err/err_all.c`'s wrapper around it. This crate transcribes the wrapper and inlines the table load, so the internal name is built by nothing while the behaviour is fully present. Recorded as reached rather than deferred, because a deferral would be false, and the same disposition holds for every `*_err.c` whose loader is generated.

The same shape as `crypto/dso/dso_err.c` with one more difference: the property library has no public `ERR_load_*_strings` at all -- `crypto/err/err_all.c` calls `ossl_err_load_PROP_strings()` directly -- so there is no export to name either. What reaches the unit is the shared loader that every one of those direct calls in err_all.c becomes, plus the reason-code table the generated module carries for `ERR_LIB_PROP`.

The name appears in the plan only to say it is not where RCU lives: *"RCU's implementation for this profile is in `crypto/threads_pthread.c` -- there is no `crypto/rcu.c`"*. The row therefore names a file that does not exist in order to record a reconnaissance finding, and the tool's "names a file the authority does not have" check is right about the fact and wrong about the intent. Recorded rather than reworded, because the sentence is worth keeping and the check must keep firing on any *other* row that invents a file. plan_reconciliation.py verifies the absence against the committed manifest, so this row fails the moment the file appears.
